articles.author: Richard Pascoe
articles.description:
I spent much of 2025 making small but consistent moves away from reliance on Big Tech. This is something I hope to complete within the next 12 months or so. I am doing this from growing privacy concerns and a desire to fully embrace the Open Source eco-system.
The fact is that I started using Open Source applications many years ago, first with LibreOffice and then with GIMP, amongst others. I'm quite lucky that I am not in an environment that demands the use of Microsoft products. It was a small move of the needle but an important one. It sowed the seeds of change.
Last year I installed Manjaro Linux on an ageing laptop and will be using Fedora KDE on my intended development machine sometime this year. Almost all of my current applications are privacy-focused and Open Source and they have not harmed my workflow in any way, shape, or form.
Even my learning has now become Open Source, thanks to excellent resources like freeCodeCamp. There are plenty of alternatives to things like VS Code out there, so I am not missing out with regards to webdev or programming. DEV Community being Open Source is one of the many reasons I joined.
This isn't a journey for everyone. There are counter-arguments that mean little to myself but would be deal-breaking for some of you. Either way, I look forward to sharing more about my journey.
articles.title: Migrating from Big Tech

I’ve written a few articles on individual new features in C23 covering attributes, auto, bool, storage classes for compound literals, constexpr, explicit underlying types for enumerations, nullptr, and typeof.  There are a few miscellaneous new features that aren’t substantial enough to warrant individual articles for each, so this article will cover them together.
You can now initialize aggregates (arrays, structures, and unions) with an empty = { }. Previously at a minimum, you had to include a 0 between the { and }.
C has had decimal, octal, and hexadecimal integer literals since its creation.  C23 adopted binary literals from C++14 using either the same 0b or 0B prefix:
int n = 0b101010;  // 42 decimal

_BitInt


A new bit-precise integer type has been added, _BitInt(n) …

articles.author: Hugo Calmels
articles.description:
When I started freelancing, I had zero agency experience, no professional network, and no client base.
But I did have something: time, grind, and curiosity.
And while everyone was building websites with WordPress, I went the opposite way — I stuck to React, Next.js, Spring Boot, and code.
I spent months digging into the CMS landscape — especially WordPress. It dominates the web, no doubt.
But something interesting happens around 2022–2023 — the growth curve plateaus. Around the same time… AI explodes.
What I realized:
Generating static sites with tools like ChatGPT has become insanely easy
You no longer need to browse Bootstrap for a simple carousel → just prompt ChatGPT, refine, and boom.
Building a simple CRUD with auth? I can spin it up in Spring Boot + React in a few hours — no CMS needed.
Yes, I rely on ChatGPT heavily. No shame. It speeds things up. You still need to know your tools.
I noticed a trend: non-tech clients using CMS like WordPress or Wix often end up looking for devs to fix or customize things.
Pages slow to load
Plugins breaking
SEO nightmares
Hard-to-scale setups
At the same time, devs (even solo) can now build cleaner, faster, SEO-friendly sites in less time — thanks to better tools, AI, and frameworks.
I mostly offer:
Custom websites (static or dynamic)
Custom web apps (dashboards, internal tools, etc.)
My stack:
Frontend: Next.js / React
Backend: Spring Boot (Java)
Hosting: Vercel, Netlify, or VPS depending on the client
Check my portfolio :
https://hugo-calmels.fr/fr
Simple: I’ve already invested in mastering multiple stacks (React, Angular, Java, etc.). Learning a CMS from scratch, with different paradigms, felt like a bad ROI.
Especially when I could start earning with what I already knew.
I'm testing the market — trying to see if small businesses and freelance clients are open to custom-coded alternatives to WordPress.
If you’re a dev doing the same, or a business tired of bloated CMS platforms, I’d love to hear from you.
articles.title: Why I Chose Custom Code Over CMS — As a Freelance Dev Starting from Scratch

articles.author: CodeCadim by Brahim Hamdouni
articles.description:
When using lf (the terminal file manager) with Kitty and Tmux, image preview display often causes issues: graphical artifacts remain on screen when switching from one preview to another, making the interface unreadable.

After several attempts, I found a solution that seems to work well. It relies on three elements:
The redraw command in lf
No cleaner script
The on-select event in lf

Here's the configuration to add to your lfrc file:
set previewer ~/.local/bin/lfpreview
cmd on-select &{{
  exec lf -remote 'send redraw'
}}


The preview script (previewer) will be detailed later. The key element here is using on-select to ask lf to redraw itself on each selection. This command performs the terminal cleanup and ensures clean preview display.
Create the file ~/.local/bin/lfpreview with the following content:
#!/bin/sh
draw() {
  kitten icat --stdin no --transfer-mode memory \
  --place "${w}x${h}@${x}x${y}" "$1" </dev/null >/dev/tty
}

file="$1"
w="$2"
h="$3"
x="$4"
y="$5"

case "$(file -Lb --mime-type "$file")" in
  image/*)
    draw "$file"
  ;;
  application/pdf)
    pdftoppm -f 1 -singlefile "$file" "/tmp/lfoutput"
    draw "/tmp/lfoutput.ppm"
  ;;
  *)
    less "$1"
  ;;
esac

exit 1 # do not cache

Don't forget to make it executable:
chmod +x ~/.local/bin/lfpreview

This simplified version handles:
Images (via kitten icat)
PDFs (converting the first page to an image)
Other files (display via less)
The exit 1 at the end of the script is crucial: it tells lf not to cache the previews. Without it, the refresh mechanism wouldn't work properly, as lf would reuse cached previews instead of redisplaying the image on each selection.
This configuration works well for my use case, but it may require adjustments depending on your environment. Feel free to adapt the preview script to handle other file types according to your needs.
articles.title: Displaying Images in lf with Kitty and Tmux

articles.author: Alex Cybercoder
articles.description:
Vibe coding is fast. It feels like magic. But magic is dangerous if you don't know how the spell works. 
In this prompt or vibe era, it is easy to get lazy and let the machine take the wheel. Don't. Your technical foundation is the only thing that keeps your project from drifting into expensive, broken territory.
AI can write a thousand lines of code in seconds, but it has no idea why it wrote them. When the "vibe" breaks, the AI usually just loops in circles. 
Your value isn't in typing the code anymore. Your value is in understanding the logic. If you can't read the stack trace, you don't own the product. You are just a passenger.
Vibe coding tools love to hide the infrastructure. They give you a "one-click" deploy that costs 10x what it should. 
If you know how to move your deployment to a basic VPS or a cheaper provider, you have sovereignty. Skills give you the power to walk away from expensive platforms. Without those skills, you are just paying a "convenience tax" every month.
Pure AI images are becoming the "junk mail" of the internet. They look perfect, but they feel empty. SEO algorithms and human readers are already starting to ignore that specific AI sheen.
Human design skills are becoming a luxury. Knowing when to break a grid or how to add a specific, intentional "imperfection" is how you stand out. Don't let your taste be averaged out by a prompt.
The machine provides the speed, but you provide the direction. Use the vibes to build fast, but keep your skills sharp so you can keep the lights on when the magic fades.
The tool is the engine. You are the anchor.
articles.title: Your skills the anchor: Staying relevant in the Vibe Era
